x=1+3t,\,y=2{t}^{3/2},\,t\in [0,1].

after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)=3\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3/2})=3{t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{(3{t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{9+9t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}(1+t)^{1/2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3\cdot {\frac{2}{3}(1+t)^{3/2}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\sqrt{8}-2 \\  & =4\sqrt{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=3cos⁡t,y=2sin⁡t from t=0 to t=π2 (shown above)?

a
∫0π/2(9sin2⁡t+4cos2⁡t)dt
b
∫0π/23sin2⁡t+2cos2⁡tdt
c
∫0π/29sin2⁡t+4cos2⁡tdt
d
∫0π/2(3sin⁡t+2cos⁡t)dt
e
∫0π/24sin2⁡t+9cos2⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: Since x′(t)=−3sin(t) and y′(t)=2cos(t), the arc-length formula gives ∫₀^{π/2}√(9sin²(t)+4cos²(t)) dt, which is option c. Option e has the same integral value by the substitution u=π/2−t; c directly matches the derivatives.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059427/assets/ca290e8fd51edddf4381ec267b8e0a5692d0e52bd2a36b7d43ab89cbeb5cf00d.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown above)?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=3cos⁡t,y=2sin⁡t from t=0 to t=π2 (shown above)?

a
∫0π/2(9sin2⁡t+4cos2⁡t)dt
b
∫0π/23sin2⁡t+2cos2⁡tdt
c
∫0π/29sin2⁡t+4cos2⁡tdt
d
∫0π/2(3sin⁡t+2cos⁡t)dt
e
∫0π/24sin2⁡t+9cos2⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(3cos⁡t)=−3sin⁡t and dydt=ddt(2sin⁡t)=2cos⁡t.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π/2(−3sin⁡t)2+(2cos⁡t)2dt=∫0π/29sin2⁡t+4cos2⁡tdt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms c: x′(t)=−3sin(t) and y′(t)=2cos(t), so integrating √(x′(t)²+y′(t)²) gives the displayed integral in c. Option e is equivalent by substituting u=π/2−t; c directly expresses the arc-length formula. The deliberately submitted option d incorrectly adds the component speeds.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059427/assets/ca290e8fd51edddf4381ec267b8e0a5692d0e52bd2a36b7d43ab89cbeb5cf00d.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown above)?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

a
∫−119sin2⁡t−8sin⁡t+64dt
b
∫−118sin2⁡t−2sin⁡t+8dt
c
∫−1110sin2⁡t−16sin⁡t+64dt
d

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′(t)=−3sin(t) and y′(t)=8−sin(t). Thus the squared speed is 9sin²(t)+(8−sin(t))²=10sin²(t)−16sin(t)+64. Integrating its square root from −1 to 1 gives option c.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=8t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t$
from $t=-1$ to $t=1$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=8-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(8-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+64-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{10{sin}^{2}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t+64}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=3cos⁡t,y=8t+cos⁡t from t=−1 to t=1 ?

a
∫−119sin2⁡t−8sin⁡t+64dt
b
∫−118sin2⁡t−2sin⁡t+8dt
c
∫−1110sin2⁡t−16sin⁡t+64dt
d
∫−11sin2⁡t−16sin⁡t+64dt
e
2∫−115sin2⁡t−8sin⁡t+32dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(3cos⁡t)=−3sin⁡t and dydt=ddt(8t+cos⁡t)=8−sin⁡t.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫−11(−3sin⁡t)2+(8−sin⁡t)2dt=∫−119sin2⁡t+64−16sin⁡t+sin2⁡tdt=∫−1110sin2⁡t−16sin⁡t+64dt.

content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=8t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t$
from $t=-1$ to $t=1$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=8-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(8-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+64-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{10{sin}^{2}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t+64}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length $L$ of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ].
$$

Do not round the answer.

$L=$
{{field-1}}
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{{(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{(2\pi )^{2}}{2}-0 \\  & =2{\pi }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
